summary:
Weather-Report turns NASA Earth science data into guided investigations for students and curious members of the public. Its rule-based discovery engine analyzes regional time series, identifies contrasting changes, and invites users to predict, check the evidence, and reason about possible explanations. An interactive globe, charts, trend rates, confidence intervals, and plain-language evidence labels help users explore what is changing, where, how quickly, and how strongly the data support that conclusion.

The project combines MERRA-2 temperature and precipitation, GLDAS soil moisture, and MODIS vegetation data. A bundled 2000–2024 dataset supports repeatable demonstrations, while additional exploration can request NASA data for selected areas and time periods. Sources and statistical methods remain visible through “How do we know?” Weather-Report addresses the challenge by bringing data acquisition, visualization, and trend analysis into one learning experience, helping users distinguish an interesting pattern from convincing evidence without treating correlation as proof of causation.
details:
What we developed

Weather-Report is an educational Earth science exploration application built for “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” It combines a Python analysis engine, a FastAPI service, and a React interface with an interactive 3D globe. Its intended audience includes high school and college students and members of the public who want to investigate environmental change without first building a data pipeline.

How it works

The project acquires NASA gridded products and reduces them into regional time series with explicit units, missing-data checks, and source metadata. The current bundled dataset contains 92 monthly series across 25 catalog regions for January 2000 through December 2024: temperature and precipitation for all 25, and soil moisture and vegetation index for 21 land regions. Land-only quantities are excluded from the ocean and ice regions where they are not offered.

The discovery engine removes the seasonal cycle and estimates linear trends, including rates per decade and 95% confidence intervals. It checks the results against annual-anomaly fits, robust regression, outlier sensitivity, Theil–Sen estimation, and Mann–Kendall testing. Autocorrelation and multiple-comparison corrections inform the evidence labels. The engine ranks regional contrasts and creates explanations from templates; it does not require an LLM at runtime.

“Surprise Me!” selects an eligible discovery. “Become a Detective” turns it into three steps: predict which region is changing faster, check the measurements and trend estimates, and reason about possible causes. “How do we know?” exposes the period, sources, statistical methods and evidence. Possible causes are context for discussion, not causal findings established by the analysis.

“Compare Regions” lets users compare a shared variable for two catalog regions. “Explore My World” supports multiple variables, drawn areas, aggregation choices, and monthly, daily or three-hourly views where the source supports them. Requests outside the bundled data can run as background acquisition jobs and use a cache; finer resolutions have period limits. Live access depends on Earthdata credentials and source availability. The separate Python/API processing layer supports arithmetic, scaling, resampling, explicit missing-value handling, temporal filtering, detrending and exploratory Pearson correlation.

Demonstrated example

The bundled Sahara–Sahel discovery compares temperature from 2000–2024. Its stored estimates are approximately +0.242 °C/decade for the Sahara, with a 95% interval of +0.051 to +0.434 and “Strong evidence,” and −0.204 °C/decade for the Sahel, with a 95% interval of −0.404 to −0.005 and “Some evidence.” These refer to the project's defined regional boxes and analysis period. The different labels show why a slope or interval alone is not the entire evidence assessment.

Benefits and intended impact

The intended benefit is scientific and statistical literacy: users practice asking a question, making a prediction, inspecting evidence, and revising an explanation. Automatic discovery lowers the barrier of choosing a starting variable and region. Transparent uncertainty makes weak evidence part of the lesson. Bundled real-data results make demonstrations repeatable without a live download. These are intended benefits, not measured learning outcomes.
Tools and implementation

The backend uses Python, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI, Uvicorn, netCDF4 and pyhdf. The frontend uses JavaScript, React, Vite and react-globe.gl. JSON Schema defines the data contracts. NASA CMR and Earthdata support discovery and authenticated acquisition. pytest and Playwright support automated checks; Git and GitHub support collaboration. No specialized hardware is required beyond a computer and browser; the 3D globe needs WebGL. Full attributions are in resources.md.

Creativity and design considerations

The central creative choice is to turn automatically discovered contrasts into a prediction-led investigation rather than leaving users with an unexplained chart. Geography, multiple Earth system variables, uncertainty and source traceability are connected in a single workflow. The team’s implementation accounts for seasonal variation, missing observations, land masks, calendar-aware precipitation conversions, repeated comparisons, autocorrelation, caching and safe handling of Earthdata credentials. The current automatic model describes linear trends; it does not forecast future conditions or establish causation.
